name: XQuAD
summary: The same 240 Wikipedia paragraphs and 1,190 reading comprehension questions in twelve languages, 14,280 question-answer pairs in all, each answered by a span of its paragraph.
overview:
XQuAD, the Cross-lingual Question Answering Dataset, asks the same reading comprehension questions in twelve languages. Each task gives a paragraph from an English Wikipedia article and a question about it, and the answer is a span of that paragraph. The dataset is entirely parallel: 240 paragraphs and 1,190 questions were taken from the SQuAD v1.1 development set and translated, paragraph and question together, into Spanish, German, Greek, Russian, Turkish, Arabic, Vietnamese, Thai, Chinese, and Hindi, with Romanian added later. A model is therefore measured on the same comprehension problems in every language, so differences in its scores reflect the language rather than the questions. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.11856)

The dataset was released in 2019 by Mikel Artetxe, Sebastian Ruder, and Dani Yogatama with a study of how monolingual models transfer across languages. The cross-lingual benchmarks available then were sentence classification tasks; the authors wanted a harder test, and released XQuAD as what they call a more comprehensive cross-lingual benchmark. XQuAD is intended for zero-shot evaluation: a model is trained on the English SQuAD v1.1 training set and then evaluated in the other eleven languages without seeing any training data in them. It became one of the question-answering tasks in the XTREME suite of cross-lingual benchmarks. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.11856) and [XTREME paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.11080)

The authors' own baselines show how much the language matters. Fine-tuned on English and evaluated zero-shot, multilingual BERT scored 83.5 F1 in English but 65.2 on average across the eleven languages, falling to 42.7 in Thai; XLM-R Large scored 86.5 in English and 77.2 on average, with Chinese its weakest language at 59.3. [Repository README](https://github.com/google-deepmind/xquad/blob/7d30520c717524000f0d9d2f9c10a069acd9d285/README.md#baselines)
methodology:
This snapshot contains all twelve language files at the pinned commit: 1,190 question-answer pairs in each of Arabic, Chinese, English, German, Greek, Hindi, Romanian, Russian, Spanish, Thai, Turkish, and Vietnamese, or 14,280 tasks. Each file holds the same 240 paragraphs, five drawn at random from each of the 48 articles in the SQuAD v1.1 development set, in SQuAD's own JSON format. Every question has exactly one reference answer, and in every language that answer appears verbatim in its paragraph at the recorded offset, which the importer checks. [Language files at the pinned commit](https://github.com/google-deepmind/xquad/tree/7d30520c717524000f0d9d2f9c10a069acd9d285)

The translations were made by professional translators from Gengo, who received the paragraph together with all of its questions, with paragraphs and questions from one article kept in the same batch for consistency. To keep the answers extractive, the authors marked the most frequent English answer inside the paragraph with placeholder symbols and asked translators to keep those symbols in place in their translation, so the answer span survives translation rather than being translated separately. Translators were told to transliterate named entities following Wikipedia's conventions, and had a validator to check the format of their output. English SQuAD development questions carry three answers from different annotators; XQuAD keeps the single marked one, which is why each task here has one reference answer. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.11856)

The Romanian file was added to the repository in January 2021 and is not part of the original ten-language release; it comes from LiRo, a benchmark of Romanian language tasks. It is imported here because it is part of the official dataset at the pinned revision. [LiRo](https://lirobenchmark.github.io/)

Each Task Prompt is the question, a line naming the source Wikipedia article, and the paragraph, all in that file's language, following the layout this catalog uses for SQuAD 2.0. The Solution is the reference answer. IDs combine the language code with the upstream SQuAD question ID, which XQuAD repeats across all twelve files, so the parallel versions of one question share an ID suffix: for example ar-56beb4343aeaaa14008c925b and th-56beb4343aeaaa14008c925b are the Arabic and Thai versions of the same question.

The English file is SQuAD v1.1 development content, unchanged: all 1,190 questions, paragraphs, article titles, and answers were found in dataset/dev-v1.1.json of rajpurkar/SQuAD-explorer. 817 of those questions also appear in the SQuAD 2.0 development set stored in this catalog as its own benchmark, so the catalog holds them twice, once in each benchmark's snapshot. No records were dropped or reworded. Unlike SQuAD 2.0, XQuAD has no unanswerable questions; the authors left them out so that models could focus on cross-lingual transfer. The importer uses only Python's standard library and can be rerun with python3 data/xquad/import.py. [SQuAD v1.1 development set](https://github.com/rajpurkar/SQuAD-explorer/blob/eee5fdbf62f8613a7812b03419e6b29617b74fd1/dataset/dev-v1.1.json)
scoring:
XQuAD is scored with the official SQuAD v1.1 evaluation script, which reports exact match, the share of questions where the answer string matches the reference exactly, and F1, the overlap between the words of the answer and the words of the reference. Both are computed after lowercasing, removing punctuation, and dropping the English articles a, an, and the, and F1 compares whitespace-separated tokens. The authors use that English script for every language, noting that language-specific normalisation heuristics changed results only marginally. A model's XQuAD result is usually reported per language and as the average across them. [Repository README](https://github.com/google-deepmind/xquad/blob/7d30520c717524000f0d9d2f9c10a069acd9d285/README.md#training-and-evaluation) and [SQuAD v1.1 evaluation script](https://github.com/allenai/bi-att-flow/blob/498c8026d92a8bcf0286e2d216d092d444d02d76/squad/evaluate-v1.1.py)

The comparison the dataset is built for is zero-shot transfer: train on the English SQuAD v1.1 training set, validate on its development set, and evaluate on the eleven other languages without training data in them. The authors also report two translation-based alternatives for context, translate-train, where the English training set is machine-translated into the target language, and translate-test, where the XQuAD test set is machine-translated into English; they note that translate-test results are not directly comparable because a small share of test examples is dropped. Any claim about XQuAD should state which setting and which training data were used. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.11856)

Benchopedia stores the paragraphs, questions, and reference answers. It does not run the evaluation script or publish model scores for this snapshot.
limitations:
The metrics were built for English. Exact match and F1 strip English articles and split answers on whitespace, which is not how Thai or Chinese text is written, so a correct answer can be scored unfairly in the languages where models already score lowest. Each question also has a single reference answer, instead of the three annotators' answers that English SQuAD development questions carry, so a correct answer phrased with different boundaries, such as including or omitting a title, counts as wrong more often than in SQuAD. [Repository README](https://github.com/google-deepmind/xquad/blob/7d30520c717524000f0d9d2f9c10a069acd9d285/README.md#training-and-evaluation)

The content is translated, and translation leaves its own marks. The paragraphs are translations of English Wikipedia text, chosen by the SQuAD authors for an English dataset, so the questions test reading a translation rather than reading what a speaker of that language would encounter; named entities were transliterated by instruction, and the authors note that different parts of the dataset may have been translated by different translators and report no separate quality assessment of the translations. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.11856)

The dataset is also small and narrow. 240 paragraphs from 48 Wikipedia articles, five per article, carry all 1,190 questions, so topic coverage is thin and scores move with the particular articles chosen. Every answer is a span of the given paragraph and every question is answerable, so nothing here tests abstention, multi-paragraph retrieval, or reasoning across documents.

Finally, the data is public and widely used, and its English half is the SQuAD v1.1 development set, one of the most reproduced files in natural language processing. The authors ask that XQuAD be used only at the end of experimentation to avoid overfitting, but there is no canary string or held-out portion, so a model may have seen the paragraphs, the questions, and the answers during training. [Repository README](https://github.com/google-deepmind/xquad/blob/7d30520c717524000f0d9d2f9c10a069acd9d285/README.md#best-practices)
